rows.description: A toddler pats a crying friend or brings a toy to comfort, showing early care. It is an emerging sign of empathy that adults reinforce with warm notice.

A school-age child sits with a lonely classmate or stands up for a friend, showing care and solidarity. Adults praise these actions and also teach how to involve an adult when the situation is unsafe.

A young adult living away from home for work misses family and friends and shows connection through calls, video chats and sharing news. Regular small contact often maintains closeness better than rare big gestures.

rows.subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
rows.description: A child learns to cry in private, breathe slowly or tell a trusted adult about hurt. Hiding sadness always is unhelpful, and long low mood with lost interest deserves adult attention.

rows.subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]
rows.description: A young adult grieving a loss far from family may feel isolated and put on a brave face. Reaching out, marking the loss through ritual and talking to friends or a counsellor supports healing.

rows.subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
rows.description: A teenager reads a friend's tears and may guess sadness, but tears also come from anger, stress, laughter and relief. Asking gently and staying present is wiser than guessing.

rows.subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
rows.subtype: Bodily signs are not lie detectors [Interpreting]
rows.description: A young adult sees someone sweat, blush or tremble in a questioning situation and wonders about guilt. These reactions occur in innocent people as well, so they must never be treated as proof.
A teenager learns that a false story about them is spreading. They feel hot shame, fear of every glance and a wish to disappear, and often cannot tell who started it.

rows.subtype: Being the subject of office talk [Receiver]
rows.description: An employee finds out that colleagues speculate about their personal life or promotion. They feel exposed and may over-manage their image, wasting energy on impressions.
A teenager who asks rhetorical questions like do you even care may be hurt, angry, sarcastic or making a point. Answering the feeling behind it works better than answering the literal words.

rows.subtype: Asking in cultures with indirect style [Mismatch]
rows.description: In some cultures direct questions feel blunt and people prefer indirect hints or asking through a third person. A young adult adapts, watching for softeners and silence that mean no.
A child who announced "I am the doctor" refuses to change the game even when it stops being fun, because going back on a spoken word feels wrong.
A student who told the class he would win the race trains harder and will not skip practice; having said it aloud, he wants his actions to match his word.

rows.subtype: Stuck in a choice already paid for [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult keeps attending a course they dislike because months and fees are spent and friends were told; consistency outweighs present judgment, and quitting feels like admitting error.
